item.title: Mets broadcaster admits being 'sick to my stomach' over Braves pitcher’s brutal outing
item.description: Keith Hernandez called it "criminal" as Braves reliever Connor Thomas surrendered 11 earned runs in a brutal outing at Citi Field against the Mets.
item.content:encoded:
Atlanta Braves reliever Connor Thomas had about as bad a day at the office as possible on Monday night against the New York Mets. In fact, it was so bad that MLB legend Keith Hernandez could barely watch what was taking place at Citi Field.

Hernandez, who has been a commentator on Mets broadcasts for nearly 30 years, was in a unique spot in the booth on Monday.

Witnessing the mightily struggling team pound Atlanta 14-3 had to have been a nice change of pace for Hernandez given the team's many inconsistencies this season, but he didn't exactly love how the team eventually got to its dominating victory.

"I'm sorry, I just think that's criminal what we just witnessed," Hernandez said during the bottom of the eighth inning.

TRUMP CAN'T HELP BUT TAKE JAB AT METS IN SPEECH WHILE PRAISING BRAVES CEO: 'THEY LOSE ALL THE TIME'

"Poor kid, you just want to give him a hug," Hernandez continued while the broadcast panned to Thomas in the Braves dugout. "Literally, I'm sick to my stomach. I'm not a happy camper."

"Criminal" may be too harsh a word to describe Thomas' outing against New York, but Hernandez feeling bad for the relief pitcher is certainly understandable.

Thomas entered the contest with things knotted up at 3-3 before giving up 10 hits, 11 earned runs, three home runs, and walking five batters in just 2.2 innings of work.

It was very much a situation that we see quite often in today's game where relievers have to stay in contests far longer than they should to preserve other arms in the bullpen.

Thomas, who retired just eight of the 23 batters he faced, was eventually replaced by a position player on the bump.

Monday night's rough go marked Thomas' second appearance on the mound for Atlanta this season. The 28-year-old came on in relief against the Pittsburgh Pirates on July 7 and allowed four runs, including one long ball, in 3.2 innings of action.

item.title: NFL star Saquon Barkley is all for MLB players fighting against salary cap: 'It should happen'
item.description: Saquon Barkley backs MLB players against the proposed salary cap, telling reporters athletes sacrifice their bodies and deserve full compensation.
item.content:encoded:
Saquon Barkley knows exactly what it's like to be stiffed in a salary-cap sport.

The Philadelphia Eagles running back rushed for 2,000 yards and won an Offensive Player of the Year Award just one season after the New York Giants decided not to pay him.

Running backs were getting the short end of the stick before a recent resurgence, as general managers felt that the position was hardly that valuable. The best are still getting paid, but there was a lot of recycling throughout the league.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

In any case, lots of difficult decisions are made in football, whereas baseball remains a non-capped sport, resulting in $700 million contracts and no cap casualties.

However, MLB owners have officially proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994 — and we all know how that turned out. The players have remained steadfast in saying that a salary cap is not negotiable, and Barkley is supporting them.

"Whatever is best for the players, I’m with that. Whatever is for the players," Barkley told Fox News Digital.

"I get how the owners have the power and stuff like this, but we go out there and sacrifice our bodies. Athletes go out there and sacrifice their bodies. I’m not under the pressure of, ‘Oh, you’re an athlete. Go out there and do what you’re told.’ I don’t get with that at all. You should be compensated for what you’re doing, and however way you should be, that’s how it should be. If that’s what they believe over there, that they should have that, and that’s going to benefit them and help them provide for their families even more, then why not? It should happen."

INSIDE MLB CBA NEGOTIATIONS AS MANFRED, PLAYERS UNION EXEC DISCUSS ISSUES AS SIDES ATTEMPT TO SAVE 2027 SEASON

Surely, Barkley and other athletes are probably a bit jealous, and he admitted he feels some responsibility as "quote-unquote, one of the faces of the league."

"I don’t know if that’s going to happen for us. I think we’ve got a little more work to do for that. We’ve got to continue to be more vocal. We’ve got to continue to educate ourselves on it. ... I need to do that. I actually had this conversation the other day with my family. But yeah, I’m all for the players, and what the players think is great for them, I agree with it," Barkley added.

MLB is likely headed to an owners' lockout if the two sides cannot agree to a new collective bargaining agreement by Dec. 1, but the salary cap is each side's top priority, and they could not be further apart on the issue.

item.title: Miami Secret Service agent charged in near-deadly fraternity hazing, officials say
item.description: A Secret Service agent allegedly served as "dean of pledges" during Kappa Alpha Psi hazing sessions that left two victims needing emergency care.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S. Secret Service agent has been arrested and charged with five felony counts, including attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, after allegedly being involved with hazing "rituals" that left two victims with life-threatening injuries.

Marquez Pinder, a 29-year-old special agent with the Miami Field Office, was ordered to be put on house arrest with a GPS tracking device.

Pinder held the title of "dean of pledges" during four, hours-long hazing sessions for a Miami chapter of the Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, according to an affidavit filed with the Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit of Florida. In that role, Pinder was allegedly involved in the hazing of two prospective members of the fraternity.

SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO

According to court records, the two victims were "paddled" and struck with "canes" by Pinder and two other fraternity members. One victim’s concern was "dismissed" by the fraternity when he reported "urinating blood" during the first hazing session, records show.

Days later, the man had to be intubated at a hospital while receiving "critical care to prevent further physical deterioration and death," a law enforcement officer reported in a sworn statement.

The other victim was treated for "blackened" and "necrotic" tissue on his buttocks from the beating, court records show. "Substantial portions of skin and soft tissue" needed to be surgically removed, and he received "extensive skin grafts to cover the areas," according to an affidavit.

AMERICA'S TOP PARTY COLLEGE HIT BY ANOTHER SEX ATTACK WEEKS AFTER BRUTAL CAMPUS RAPE CASE

His "mobility and quality of life have been significantly impacted," a law enforcement officer wrote. And without emergency medical care, "his injuries would have resulted in renal failure leading to death."

The alleged hazing occurred every day April 1-4 at two different residences in Miami-Dade County, court records show.

During the meetings, the two victims were tested with questions about the fraternity and its history, according to the affidavit. Victims told law enforcement officers that when they failed to answer a question correctly, they were placed in what they called a "stress position," the affidavit shows.

RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS

They described the "stress position" as a half-squat with one arm pointed forward. While in that position, the victims said they were "struck on their buttocks with a paddle." One of the victims said that, before the hazing, he was told that "if he ever felt that he was reaching his physical limit," he should tell Pinder, his "dean of pledges," officers reported. He said he was told that indications of reaching that limit might include urinating blood or feeling that he was going to pass out, according to the affidavit.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Investigators reported they’d reviewed messages between fraternity members about the need for cleaning supplies to "mop up sweat and blood" from the hazing. After four days of "testing" to become members of the fraternity, one victim sought emergency medical treatment because his "health continued to deteriorate, and he began to suffer from vomiting, fevers, and immense pain on his buttocks," officers reported.

SEND US A TIP

Pinder now faces five felony charges, including two counts of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, two counts of attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon and one count of hazing with a deadly weapon.

Jared James and Elijah Dyous, who allegedly helped in the hazing, face the same charges, court records show.

GOT A TIP?

The three men could not be reached for comment. An attorney reportedly representing Pinder did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.

Pinder has been employed with the U.S. Secret Service since September 2023, an agency spokesperson told Fox News Digital. Pinder is currently on administrative leave.

"The United States Secret Service takes seriously any criminal misconduct allegations involving one of our employees," said Michael Townsend, special agent in charge of the Secret Service Miami Field Office. "We are fully cooperating with the investigation."

"The Secret Service remains committed to accountability, professionalism, and integrity, and any misconduct will be addressed swiftly and appropriately upon completion of the investigative and judicial process."

Kappa Alpha Psi is described on the organization's website as a "historically African-American fraternity." The national organization was founded in 1911.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

The Richmond-Perrine Alumni Chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi is not affiliated with the University of Miami, Megan Afkham, assistant vice president of university communications, told Fox News Digital in an email.

One of the victims is a University of Miami School of Law student, Afkham said, but the chapter is not connected to the university or its undergraduate chapter.

In a written statement issued by the national Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, Jimmy McMikle, the organization’s national president, said the organization "maintains a strict zero-tolerance policy on hazing."

item.title: One of these eight college football teams will be hoisting the national championship trophy in 2026
item.description: Eight college football teams have a realistic shot at the national championship in 2026, from Ohio State and Texas to defending champion Indiana.
item.content:encoded:
At the beginning of every college football season, the age-old adage of "hope springs eternal" rings true for every fanbase.

Every team is 0-0 and all their goals for the coming year are in front of them.

Many programs, coaches, and fanbases all believe they have a chance to win a national title, and in a mathematical sense they aren't wrong.

I'm here to tell you, however, that it's rarely that wide open and, during any given year, only a handful of teams can actually win the whole thing.

This year, I've identified eight teams who I believe can hoist a national championship trophy.

MISSOURI'S ELI DRINKWITZ BECOMES LATEST SEC COACH TO MAKE RIDICULOUS COMPLAINTS ABOUT BIG TEN SCHEDULES

Through some combination of returning production, transfer portal talent, and elite coaching, one of these eight teams will more than likely be the last one standing next January.

The Ohio State Buckeyes could probably get penciled into this list every year while Ryan Day is their head coach and their talent acquisition stays at the level it's currently at, but this year in particular feels like a big one in Columbus.

Coach Day has assembled a staff consisting largely of former NFL coaches and coordinators, and the addition of offensive coordinator Arthur Smith feels like a particularly noteworthy one to keep an eye on.

The Buckeyes have been recruiting at a top-five level for the past several cycles, and have supplemented that with a small but elite transfer portal class, including bolstering their defense with the likes of Alabama defensive linemen Qua Russaw and James Smith as well as Florida State safety Earl Little Jr.

On offense, Ohio State returns what may end up being the best quarterback-wide receiver tandem in the country, as Julian Sayin looks to build on a quietly brilliant 2025 while Jeremiah Smith could be argued as the best overall player in college football.

An early test on the road against Texas as well as a rematch of the Big Ten Championship in Bloomington against the Hoosiers will tell us everything we need to know about how real the Buckeyes are in 2026.

Speaking of those Longhorns, Texas will be looking to right the wrongs from a disappointing 2025 heading into this year.

Last season, the Horns were a popular preseason national championship pick, but a less than ideal start had them on the outside looking in by season's end.

Texas will likely be near the top of the preseason polls again this year, but unlike in 2025, they know what they have in signal caller Arch Manning.

Manning's first half of last season was forgettable, but by November, you could argue he blossomed into one of the best quarterbacks in the country.

He has the weapons he needs to be truly elite, with receiver Ryan Wingo returning and wideout Cam Coleman coming over from Auburn, so there won't be any excuses for another sputtering start out of the gate in '26.

Texas' defense will be among the best in the country, and veteran leaders like edge rusher Colin Simmons and linebacker Rasheem Biles (both preseason All-Americans) will bolster a fearsome unit.

There has never been a dearth of talent in Austin, but coach Steve Sarkisian may finally have his most complete team since stepping foot on the 40 Acres, and that alone has people starting to feel like it's 2005 in Central Texas again.

The Miami Hurricanes were a fourth quarter Carson Beck interception away from winning the national championship in January, but the scary thing is they might be even more dangerous in 2026.

Head coach Mario Cristobal has built a machine in Coral Gables, and the Canes have the most talented roster they've had since the early 2000s.

That's not to say they don't have to replace some absolute studs, particularly along the lines of scrimmage, but Cristobal and co. have recruited well enough in the trenches that this may be a matter of reloading rather than rebuilding.

On the offensive side of the ball, Miami has an embarrassment of riches for offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson to tinker with.

The Canes return wide receiver Malachi Toney and running back Mark Fletcher Jr. from their CFP runner-up squad last season, and they added Duke wide receiver Cooper Barkate, who was one of the most coveted pass catchers in the portal from this past offseason.

The real prize, though, was Duke quarterback Darian Mensah.

Miami will be paying Mensah a pretty penny, but he will be worth every cent of his exorbitant paycheck, as the redshirt junior may end up being the most talented signal caller Cristobal has had while in South Florida.

The schedule is forgivable, even by ACC standards, but a rematch on the road against Notre Dame will separate the Canes as contenders or pretenders.

It's crazy that I made it halfway through the list without mentioning the defending national champions, but I think coach Curt Cignetti and crew almost like it that way.

Last year, no one outside of the locker room at Memorial Stadium thought this team had a chance to win the whole thing, but the Hoosiers won't be sneaking up on anyone this year.

Cignetti doesn't have a star-studded roster like Miami, Texas, or Ohio State, but that's never stopped him before (obviously) and the talent in Bloomington is only getting better.

The Hoosiers signed a top-ten portal class, and although it was a relatively small class (17 total players) there were some gems to be found.

Quarterback Josh Hoover comes to Indiana by way of TCU, and will look to be the next big thing in Cignetti and offensive coordinator Mike Shanahan's system.

The last transfer quarterback they took ended up becoming a Heisman winner and number 1 overall NFL Draft pick, so Hoover will hope to continue the tradition.

Former Michigan State wide receiver Nick Marsh will give Hoover an elite target to throw to and will pair nicely with returning wideout Charlie Becker, who had a brilliant 2025 campaign averaging nearly 20 yards per catch.

Indiana likely won't be tested until the midway point of the season in a home game against Ohio State, and by then the team should be firing on all cylinders for the second half of the year.

Of all the teams on this list, the LSU Tigers are the wild card and have the widest range of potential outcomes to consider.

It's no secret the Bayou Bengals went out and got Lane Kiffin to be their head coach, who can be a bit of a wildcard in his own right.

But, when Kiffin is on, he's one of the best in the business at scoring points and talking smack in the process.

Paired with Kiffin is a pair of elite coordinators in Charlie Weis Jr. (OC) and Blake Baker (DC) as well as a rumored $40 million roster.

LANE KIFFIN MAKES RIDICULOUS EXCUSES FOR SEC'S POOR RECENT PERFORMANCE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

LSU also landed the number one transfer portal class and has studs at plenty of key positions, so conventional wisdom says they will be contenders right out of the gate.

The truth of the matter is, it doesn't always work out that way, and if you told me the Tigers won a national championship or went 7-5, I'd find both outcomes equally believable.

They have the firepower and an elite coaching staff, but they also play a pretty loaded schedule, starting with Clemson Week 1 and getting two more Playoff teams from last season (Ole Miss and Texas A&M) before the calendar even flips to October.

I could easily see them stumbling out of the gate and imploding, but I could also see them catching fire early and riding that wave to the promised land.

LSU can win a national championship in 2026. The question is will they?

Things have gone about as well as one would want when it comes to coach Dan Lanning's time in Eugene.

The 40-year-old head coach is entering his fifth season with the Ducks, and his resume looks pretty stacked by any metric.

He's 48-8, captured the Big Ten title in Oregon's first year in the league, and has won 10 games or more every year he's been the coach there.

But he's missing that one thing to make his list of accomplishments feel more complete: a national championship.

While 2026 isn't championship or bust in the Pacific Northwest, some fans are starting to question if Lanning will ever get it done as a head coach, especially after last season's beatdown at the hands of Indiana in the CFP Semifinals.

This would be the year for him to slay that dragon, though, as Oregon will once again have one of the most talented teams in the country.

The Ducks and Lanning have been an absolute Death Star on the recruiting trail, and this season could be the culmination in all that hard work on the talent acquisition front.

Veteran signal caller Dante Moore eschewed the NFL Draft to come back and lead his team to a natty, and he will have two absolute weapons to throw the football to this coming year.

Sophomore Dakorien Moore, a former five-star recruit in his own right, had a very good freshman year but will be looking to take the next step in 2026, while senior Evan Stewart is back and 100% healthy and ready to show anyone who forgot about him why he was one of the most coveted players in the country when he transferred from Texas A&M two years ago.

On defense, the Ducks boast a trio of preseason All-Americans in defensive back Brandon Finney Jr., linebacker Teitum Tuioti, and defensive lineman A'Mauri Washington who will look to continue the trend of elite defensive play in Eugene.

The talent will have to rise to the top, because Lanning will be replacing both coordinators, as DC Tosh Lupoi and OC Will Stein departed for head coaching jobs at Cal and Kentucky, respectively.

When Brian Kelly departed South Bend for Baton Rouge nearly five years ago, I thought Notre Dame had seen their peak as a football program in the modern era.

Always the bridesmaid but never the bride, I figured new head coach Marcus Freeman would, at best, keep them in that 10-win/CFP first round exit realm.

Little did I know the former defensive coordinator turned full time head coach would prove me so wrong.

Two years ago, Freeman had the Irish on the doorstep of a national championship, and after a minor setback in 2025, the Golden Domers look to be right back in the thick of things.

This might be Freeman's most talented group of players yet, and it all starts with quarterback CJ Carr.

The offseason buzz around this young man has been Manningesque, and his growth over the second half of last season should be enough proof that those words aren't just hot air.

The Irish have also started recruiting at a championship level, and that should start to bear fruit as early as this season, as Freeman's efforts on the trail have considerably raised both the floor and ceiling of talent on this roster.

Having to replace two first-round draft picks at running back in Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price will be a tall ask, but I think the sum will be greater than the parts for Notre Dame in 2026 and, aside from their opener against Wisconsin, the team will be able to ease into their schedule before their ultimate test on Nov. 7 against Miami.

No list of national championship contenders is complete without Kirby Smart and the Georgia Bulldogs, but they aren't making this roster of teams on the merits of their logo alone.

Georgia recruits better than almost anyone in the country, and the 2026 edition of this roster will feature a ton of former big-time prospects who waited their turn and were developed the old-fashioned way.

That includes quarterback Gunner Stockton, who has a ton of experience and a very solid 2025 campaign to build off of.

The third-team All-SEC selection will have a familiar face in offensive coordinator Mike Bobo coaching him up and will be able to lean on a fantastic running back in Nate Frazier as well as a trio of all-conference offensive linemen.

The defense will look to return to form as a vintage Kirby Smart unit, led by defensive backs KJ Bolden and Ellis Robinson, both of whom were tabbed as preseason first-team All-SEC selections by the media.

The Dawgs have a tricky six-game stretch in the middle of the season, starting at home against Oklahoma and featuring road games against Alabama and Ole Miss along the way.

It remains to be seen just how high the ceiling will be for this Georgia team in 2026, but they have the requisite talent and a coach who has been to the mountaintop twice in recent history, so count the Bulldogs out at your own risk.

item.title: Heart-shaped Las Vegas resort gets green light as critics roast wild design online
item.description: The Clark County Zoning Commission approved a massive heart-shaped resort on 12 acres near Mandalay Bay on the Strip. Many online commenters are roasting the design.
item.content:encoded:
Nevada officials unanimously approved plans for a heart-shaped resort hotel and recreational venue on the far south end of the Las Vegas Strip — and the unusual design is already attracting plenty of attention online. 

The Clark County Zoning Commission unanimously approved plans for the proposed heart-shaped resort last week, Fox 5 Las Vegas reported.

The development is proposed on about 12 acres east of Las Vegas Boulevard South, between Mandalay Bay Road and Four Seasons Drive near Haven Street.

BARGAIN BUFFET REFUSES TO DIE WHILE LUXURY DINING TAKES OVER VEGAS

Planners trimmed the project's scope to a height of 317 feet and 752 hotel rooms, down from the original proposal of 406 feet and 874 rooms, according to industry publication NVBEX.

Renderings show the project — which doesn't have an official public name yet — centered around a massive, illuminated heart-shaped hotel tower, with a casino, restaurants and retail space spread across the base of the development.

Fox News Digital reached out to Steelman Partners, the project's architectural firm, for comment.

The concept is planned as a "pedestrian entertainment corridor," Fox 5 Las Vegas reported.

During the meeting, officials said the site has changed little since the early 2000s, after a previous proposal to build a Ferris wheel stalled.

LAS VEGAS OFFICIALS WEIGH BANNING CRIMINAL OFFENDERS FROM STRIP TO REVIVE TOURISM

On a Reddit forum dedicated to Las Vegas, reactions to the proposal were mixed, with many users criticizing or mocking the design.

"It honestly looks so ugly," one person wrote.

"We just need a diamond, spade and club hotel," another joked.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

A third user wrote, "This design would make a great 3-story wedding chapel, but not a 29-story hotel."

Others embraced the over-the-top concept.

"I like this better than the guitar," one commenter wrote, an apparent reference to the guitar-shaped Hard Rock Hotel currently under construction on the Strip and set to replace the Mirage.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"It better bring back heart-shaped tubs and those heart-shaped love beds," another person quipped. 

"You guys wanted more theme[d] hotels," another person said. "Here you go."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The proposal comes as Las Vegas continues its shift toward a more upscale tourism market, with luxury hotels, premium dining and major events playing a larger role in the city’s economy.

That transformation has also brought higher costs for visitors, with travelers increasingly voicing frustration over resort fees, expensive meals and rising hotel prices, Fox News Digital previously reported.

item.title: DEI hiring boost for one blue state's Muslim commission initiative flies in face of Trump's anti-woke push
item.description: Massachusetts lawmakers advance a bill to create a permanent Muslim commission as Trump moves to dismantle DEI programs across the federal government.
item.content:encoded:
Massachusetts lawmakers are taking steps toward prioritizing the hiring of American Muslims for state government positions under a permanent so-called Muslim commission.

The group would help recommend Americans who practice Islam to appointed government positions in the New England state at the same time the Trump administration is moving to dismantle such diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs nationwide — teeing-up a standoff between local leaders and the president.

A proposed bill would create a panel of 11 Muslims appointed by Democratic Gov. Maura Healey and other state officials to represent the Islamic faith on issues such as business, economy, healthcare and other concerns.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST ACTRESS CYNTHIA NIXON HANDED POWERFUL ROLE IN HELPING CHOOSE NEW YORK TOP JUDGES

The Muslim commission would influence government recruiting and, "Identify and recommend qualified American Muslims for appointive positions at all levels of government, including boards and commissions, as the commission considers necessary and appropriate," according to language in the bill.

"Massachusetts has always prided itself on being a leader in equality and civil rights, a legacy this bill builds upon," said Democratic state Sen. Jamie Eldridge, the bill's primary sponsor.

"American Muslims in my district and across the Commonwealth enrich our communities as students, healthcare workers, educators, small business owners, and civic leaders," Eldridge added in the press release on the proposal. "This commission will help the state better understand and address the challenges they face, while strengthening inclusion and civic participation. "

Senate Bill S.2134 currently sits in the state's Senate Ways and Means Committee after clearing initial committee markups and votes.

Muslims account for an estimated 2% to 3% of Massachusetts' population, according to approximate figures from Pew Research Center and the U.S. Census.

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

Massachusetts' push comes as President Donald Trump has made it a mission of his administration to cut back on DEI programs in the private sector, as well as in the federal government.

"President Trump was resoundingly elected with a mandate to end divisive, racist policies and restore merit and efficiency," White House spokesperson Allison Shuster told Fox News Digital.

"DEI ran rampant during the Biden Administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs, and workforce inefficiencies," Shuster added. "The Trump Administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity."

The president's team has terminated federal DEI-related contracts and eliminated DEI federal government programs.

Part of Trump's initiative during his first 100 days with the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) was to put an end to programs that prioritized hiring and representation in the workplace based on applicants' protected classes.

Many Republicans, including the president and Musk, claimed that DEI was "reverse discrimination" that provided unfair preferences against majority groups in the U.S.

Gov. Healey's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the legislation.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Biden pardon won't shield Fauci if he lies to Congress, Comer says
item.description: Rep. James Comer warns Dr. Anthony Fauci that former President Biden's pardon has limits ahead of his Senate hearing, saying he must be held accountable if he lies.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., is warning Dr. Anthony Fauci that his presidential pardon has limits ahead of the former public health official's high-profile day on Capitol Hill.

Fauci is set to testify before a GOP-led Senate panel on Wednesday, days after hundreds of pages of his COVID-19 pandemic-era diary entries were made public.

"We now know why President Biden gave a blanket pardon to Dr. Fauci. While obsessing about his own fame, Dr. Fauci wasn't truthful with the American people about the origins of COVID and advised schools to be closed," Comer told Fox News Digital.

LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

"Americans are still reaping the consequences of Dr. Fauci's actions. Biden's pardon doesn't cover Dr. Fauci's testimony this week and if he continues to lie, he must be held accountable."

Fauci was among several recipients of controversial "preemptive pardons" by former President Joe Biden made during the final hours of the Democratic administration.

The pardon covers any offenses from January 1, 2014, through its issue date, or anything related "to his service as Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, as a member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or the White House COVID-19 Response Team, or as Chief Medical Advisor to the President."

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Because the pardon covers conduct during his government service, there will likely be some debate over whether it would protect him from liability stemming from his testimony.

But other House Republicans are also accusing Fauci of behaving in a way that hurts public trust in U.S. health, including the co-chairs of the House GOP Doctors' Caucus — both of whom are physicians themselves.

"Dr. Fauci, enamored with his own fame and vanity, put politics above science during the pandemic. He is primarily responsible for the resulting multi-generational erosion of trust in American medicine," Rep. Greg Murphy, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital. "A perfect example of ego destroying whatever achievements he had prior to the pandemic."

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Rep. John Joyce, R-Pa., told Fox News Digital that Fauci "must be held accountable" by the House as well as the Senate.

"The release of Dr. Fauci's diary entries validates what many Americans suspected all along: he was not honest about the origins of COVID-19," Joyce said. "His fixation on preserving his own image and maintaining a position of power eroded public trust, undermined the integrity of our public health institutions, and failed the American people."

Diary entries made public by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., a longtime Fauci critic and chair of the committee before which Fauci is appearing on Wednesday, show the high-profile doctor reflecting on his pandemic-era fame and raising questions about the disease's origins.

Some entries appear to show Fauci taking credit for influencing policies that closed schools during the pandemic, something that has become one of the most hotly debated aspects of how the government handled COVID.

He told the House Oversight Committee in January 2024, however, "I did not close the schools."

Fauci has long denied any wrongdoing and instead has argued that he's been made a political target by people on the right who are critical of how governments handled COVID-19.

item.title: Phillies vs. Marlins betting preview: Aaron Nola's struggles meet Sandy Alcantara's home ERA edge
item.description: Aaron Nola's 5.82 ERA faces Sandy Alcantara's strong 3.26 home ERA as the Phillies visit Miami with both teams struggling since the All-Star break.
item.content:encoded:
I took two losses yesterday, and both were on coinflip games. I acknowledged that in both articles, and unfortunately, we couldn't get the games to bounce our way. Neither one of the games was a blowout loss or bad choices. The teams just didn't get the wins that I was expecting them to get. Instead, we lost both games 3-2. Let us try to dodge that fate here as we take on the Phillies and Marlins.

The Philadelphia Phillies seem to have cooled off a bit after their hot stretch. They aren't playing poorly by any means, but they just aren't quite as successful as they had been. In July, they are just 9-12 and have lost five of their past six games. Maybe they just need to find a groove after the All-Star Break because they have gone 3-7 in the second half. item.title: Flock surveillance spreads across the South as red-state lawmakers seek to axe '1984'-style tracking tools
item.description: West Virginia's Freedom Caucus seeks to ban Flock Safety cameras statewide, calling automated license plate readers a Fourth Amendment violation.
item.content:encoded:
State lawmakers in West Virginia's Freedom Caucus are seeking to ban AI-powered Flock surveillance cameras statewide, arguing the technology violates citizens' Fourth Amendment right to privacy.

"The West Virginia Freedom Caucus strongly opposes the unchecked expansion of automated surveillance technologies, including Flock Safety camera systems, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), AI-powered facial recognition, multimodal vehicle recognition, and emerging 'gun detection' software that claims to identify armed citizens based on body shape or movement," West Virginia Delegate Chris Anders, the Chairman of West Virginia's Freedom Caucus, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"These technologies represent a dramatic expansion of government surveillance that is fundamentally at odds with the Fourth Amendment," Anders added.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

"No state or local government should be mass tracking the daily movements of law-abiding citizens without a warrant. Mass surveillance has no place in a free society," Anders also said in a statement posted to the caucus' X account.

The caucus is calling on all state municipalities to immediately remove automated license plate readers such as the ones run by the security company Flock Safety.

"The Constitution does not disappear because technology advances," Anders added.

The caucus plans on combatting the cameras and surveillance technologies by reintroducing a previously failed legislative measure called the Fourth Amendment Restoration Act.

The bill would prohibit a series of AI-powered surveillance technologies from being used by law enforcement and other agencies in the state. The technologies it would ban include facial recognition software, surveillance drones, license plate readers and more.

"For two consecutive years, the Fourth Amendment Restoration Act has been introduced in the West Virginia Legislature, yet it has failed to reach the Governor's desk. That must change," Anders also said, placing blame for the bill's previous failures at the feet of the state's legislative leadership.

"Despite growing public concern over government surveillance, Speaker Roger Hanshaw and House Judiciary Chairman JB Akers declined to bring the bill forward for consideration. As a result, the House was never given the opportunity to debate or vote on the legislation," Anders wrote in an email to Fox News Digital.

"If House leadership continues to deny the people's elected representatives the opportunity to vote on this fundamental constitutional issue, the Freedom Caucus will use every parliamentary tool available to insist that the Fourth Amendment Restoration Act receive an up-or-down vote in both chambers. Constitutional rights should never be quietly buried in committee," Anders added.

Chairman Akers, in a response to Anders' comments, told Fox News Digital, "We actually passed a bill last session that limits the amount of surveillance law enforcement may engage in on private property. Unfortunately, Chris Anders submits sloppily drafted bills given to him by outside groups. In the 4th Amendment context, his proposals would prevent even normal law enforcement actions that conservatives support."

"Last session, he tried to amend a bill in a way that would have prevented police from entering property even if a dead body were in plain view in the front yard. Bluntly, his idea was dumb," Akers said of Anders' proposal draft. "He left me no choice but to say that. If he’s going to blame others for failing to get his bills through, then he needs to do better work. Frankly, I think he’d rather see his bad bills fail so he can then scream RINO for clicks."

Other Freedom Caucus members also objected to the Flock cameras.

"The Fourth Amendment was written specifically to stop the government from engaging in generalized surveillance and warrantless searches," West Virginia Freedom Caucus Secretary Henry Dillon said in a statement. He argued that "Flock cameras don't just identify criminals — they create a database documenting where law-abiding citizens worship, seek medical care, conduct business, and travel."

"That is fundamentally incompatible with a free society," he said.

JOHNSON FACES GOP REVOLT OVER WARRANTLESS SURVEILLANCE POWERS AHEAD OF KEY VOTE

Another Freedom Caucus member, state Sen. Craig Hart, pointed to a series of alleged police abuses involving Flock cameras in Georgia, including a 2025 incident in which Braselton Police Department Chief Michael Steffman was arrested for allegedly using automated license plate readers to stalk and harass people.

According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Atlas of Surveillance, at least five West Virginia municipalities incorporate Flock Safety license plate readers, while other municipalities like Wheeling and the state capital of Charleston operate drones, camera registries and intelligence fusion centers.

The American Civil Liberties Union is suing the West Virginia city of Huntington after its mayor and city council agreed to a $2.1 million deal with Flock for AI-powered surveillance equipment.

"If the Court allows the contract to proceed, Huntington would be blanketed in license plate recognition cameras with vehicle fingerprint technology, live video cameras, gunshot detection audio devices, and even automatically dispatched drones," the ACLU wrote in a statement.

The ACLU said more than 50 citizens attended the city council meeting to voice their disapproval of the agreement.

Meanwhile, Huntington Mayor Patrick Farrell argued that Flock cameras in other states have already helped catch West Virginia suspects.

Recounting a pursuit of a murder suspect who allegedly shot a woman in the head near Huntington, Farrell said "he was going back to Michigan, and luckily for us, some other city had license plate reader cameras that caught the car."

"That gave us the lead that led to his arrest in Michigan. So it helps our law enforcement do its work faster, more efficiently, and that’s the kind of success that I think we need more of," the mayor said.

Despite the safety argument, Anders and his caucus insist the technology violates the Constitution.

"The Founders did not fight a revolution so government could monitor innocent citizens everywhere they travel," Anders told Fox News Digital. "George Orwell's 1984 was intended as a warning, not an instruction manual. We should be striving for more 1776, not more 1984."

"The Fourth Amendment Restoration Act does not prevent police from investigating crime. It simply requires government to do what the Constitution has required for over two centuries: obtain a warrant based upon probable cause before engaging in targeted surveillance of Americans," Anders concluded.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Flock Safety maintained that the company protects personal privacy and claimed to support legislation that sets guardrails for license plate readers.

"Flock strongly supports legislation that creates clear guardrails for how license plate recognition data is used and shared, while preserving the effectiveness of an important public safety tool," a company spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement. "These systems play a critical role in helping law enforcement solve crimes, locate missing people, and keep communities safe. Taking away or weakening access to this technology would have real consequences for public safety. We believe the right approach is not to eliminate an effective tool, but to regulate it responsibly. State lawmakers should establish strong safeguards that ensure accountability, oversight, and responsible use, while preserving the ability of law enforcement to use these technologies in ways that communities expect and rely on. We stand ready to be a resource as lawmakers consider these important issues."

"Flock customers retain full ownership and control of their data. Flock does not sell data. Access is limited to authorized users, and agencies determine whether to share data with other law enforcement agencies through opt-in sharing relationships that they can change or revoke at any time. Data is automatically deleted after 30 days by default," the company spokesperson concluded.

Fox News Digital also contacted Morrisey and Hanshaw for comment but did not immediately hear back.

item.title: Golden Dome could leave US vulnerable to drone attacks without Israeli systems
item.description: A new report warns Golden Dome's focus on space-based missile defense could leave U.S. cities vulnerable to drone attacks over the homeland.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: As Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets President Donald Trump in Washington for talks expected to center on Iran and regional security, a new report is urging the administration to expand U.S.–Israel defense cooperation by making Israeli air-defense technology a central component of the Golden Dome, the planned layered missile shield intended to detect, track and intercept ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, hypersonic weapons and drones before they can strike the United States.

The report warns that the planned American missile shield could leave U.S. cities, military installations and critical infrastructure exposed to increasingly common drone and cruise-missile threats if Washington directs too much money toward costly space-based systems that could take years to become operational.

The Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) report, titled "The Missing Shield: Acquiring Israeli Air Defenses Makes Golden Dome Sustainable," argues that the initiative’s current funding priorities favor strategic and space-based capabilities that could take years to develop while giving insufficient attention to more frequent, lower-altitude threats such as drones, cruise missiles and shorter-range projectiles.

THE US-ISRAEL STRATEGIC ALLIANCE – PARTNERSHIP, NOT CHARITY

Ari Cicurel, the report’s author, told Fox News Digital that long-range defenses remain necessary but should not come at the expense of systems capable of stopping threats that could reach the United States now.

"Right now, the current approach is spending the time and money primarily on space, long-range threats, which are absolutely needed," Cicurel said. "But the most frequent and immediate threats are actually short-range projectiles, particularly drones."

Cicurel pointed to recent drone activity over American cities, including Washington, D.C., as evidence that the danger is not confined to overseas battlefields.

"We’ve seen several drone overflights of cities, including in Washington, D.C., over the past few months," he said. "And that’s certainly the most frequent threat that the U.S. needs to be addressing."

The report estimates that the Israeli-designed launchers it examined are 58% to 88% less expensive, interceptors 19% to 97% less expensive and radars 32% to 87% less expensive than the U.S. systems used for comparison. JINSA argues those savings could allow the Pentagon to purchase more launchers, expand interceptor stockpiles and preserve funding for expensive strategic and space-based technologies.

The Pentagon told Fox News Digital that Golden Dome is being designed as a layered system capable of addressing a broad range of threats.

"Golden Dome for America continues to focus its efforts on protecting America and delivering on President Trump’s vision for homeland defense," a Pentagon official said.

PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSHES RAPID UNMANNED WARFARE EXPANSION

The official said the implementation plan remains "dynamic" and is intended to defend against "the full spectrum of evolving threats," including hypersonic and ballistic missiles, advanced cruise missiles and unmanned aerial systems.

The scale of the choices ahead was underscored by a May 12 Congressional Budget Office analysis. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that a notional national missile-defense system broadly consistent with Trump’s executive order could cost approximately $1.2 trillion over 20 years to develop, deploy and operate. 

The office stressed that the estimate was not a projection of the Pentagon’s actual Golden Dome plan because the department had not released sufficient details about its intended architecture.

The Congressional Budget Office modeled four interceptor layers, including a space-based layer, two wide-area surface layers and a regional surface-defense layer.

The JINSA report proposes making Israeli-designed defenses a central part of those lower layers. It recommends Iron Dome for short-range threats, David’s Sling for medium-range threats, Arrow for ballistic missiles and Iron Beam for lower-cost laser interception.

JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA

Cicurel said the proposal should not be seen simply as buying foreign weapons because Washington helped finance their development and American companies already participate in their production.

"What we’re really talking about is finally leveraging American tax dollars that have gone to help produce, help develop these Israeli systems," he said.

One hundred and two companies across 34 states participate in producing Israeli air defense systems.

Asked specifically whether the Pentagon is evaluating Iron Dome, David’s Sling, Arrow or Iron Beam for purchase, integration or expanded co-production, the official declined to say.

"We have nothing new to announce at this time," the official said. "Due to operational security and the need to protect our competitive advantages, we will not provide further details."

The report also argues that recent fighting with Iran demonstrated how high interception rates can obscure vulnerabilities, including rapid depletion of interceptor inventories, strained production lines and attacks against radar systems anchoring defensive networks.

"Both the U.S. and the Israeli defense industrial bases were not well-equipped to handle the amount of production that either country needed," Cicurel said.

The report calls for dedicated Golden Dome funding for short- and medium-range defenses, expanded joint production, and the inclusion of Golden Dome cooperation in the next U.S.-Israel memorandum of understanding. It also recommends updating export-control and technology-sharing rules, while acknowledging challenges involving interoperability, classified data and intellectual property.

Trump has repeatedly described the Golden Dome as a defining homeland-defense project, saying it would create a shield capable of protecting the United States from advanced missile threats. Whether Israeli systems become part of that architecture remains unclear, but Netanyahu’s visit gives both governments an opportunity to push the issue higher on the bilateral defense agenda.

Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who at the time had just spent a day traveling with Biden, insisted that he was, "at the very top of his game, all the way through it, both in private and in person."

item.title: Shaquille O'Neal offers rebuttal for NBA fans claiming LeBron James is 'ring chasing' by joining Sixers
item.description: Shaquille O'Neal defends LeBron James against ring chaser criticism, comparing the Philadelphia 76ers move to his own final season with Boston Celtics.
item.content:encoded:
It goes without saying that LeBron James would like to win another NBA title before retiring, which is the same goal that every single player in the Association has. That fact hasn't slowed down the criticism of James' decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers, with many labeling him a "ring chaser" for taking his talents to Philly.

James, who will turn 42 in December, has four NBA championship rings to his name, having won them with three different teams. It's very easy to argue that his choice to join the Sixers as opposed to other suitors such as the Miami Heat, Cleveland Cavaliers, and Golden State Warriors does give him the best and perhaps easiest path to pick up another title, which leads back to the ring-chasing title he's picked up since making his decision.

If we're honest, James would have been labeled a ring chaser no matter what franchise he signed with simply based on his age and the fact that he's on the tail end of his career.

PHILADELPHIA ATHLETES, INCLUDING NEW TEAMMATES, REACT TO LEBRON JAMES JOINING 76ERS: 'WELCOME TO THE CITY'

Basketball Hall of Famer Shaquille O'Neal knows a thing or two about carrying around the same label of ring chaser after joining the Boston Celtics in the final season of his career. James receiving similar treatment before suiting up for the Sixers doesn't exactly sit well with him, however.

"I don't like y'all calling my man a ring chaser," O'Neal said, referring to James, during a recent appearance on "The Stephen A. Smith Show."

"It's funny to me that people that don't have rings to say 'Oh, he's a ring chaser.' No, he's continuous chasing, he's chasing the chance to continue to be great, to continue to add legacy to his book.

"When this thing is over, it's over, you can't come back. Once you retire, once your body says it can't go no more, it's over. This guy feels he has two or three years left, why not try and get another championship? I did it, I did it with Boston. I won three in a row and then won one in Miami. At the end of my career, let me go play with Paul [Pierce] and KG (Kevin Garnett) and see if I can win one."

THE 76ERS JUMP TO BETTING FAVORITE OUT EAST AFTER LEBRON JAMES TAKES HIS TALENTS TO PHILADELPHIA

James will be teaming up alongside Joel Embiid, Jaylen Brown, and Tyrese Maxey in Philadelphia, which could evolve into a certified four-headed monster in the Eastern Conference.

The most important word in the previous sentence, however, is 'could.'

Ring chaser, or 'continious chaser' as O'Neal put it, the labels and even the predictions don't matter at this point. The only thing that does matter is what James and the Sixers do come April of next year when the postseason starts.

item.title: Wearable patch vibrates when danger is nearby
item.description: NC State researchers built a solar-powered wearable patch with six sensors that vibrates against your skin using distinct haptic alerts for each hazard.
item.content:encoded:
Your phone can warn you about bad weather or heavy traffic. However, some dangers cannot wait for you to notice a notification. A hazardous gas may already surround you. Contaminated water may look perfectly normal. By the time you unlock your phone and check an alert, you could have already spent valuable time near the threat.

Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable patch that takes the phone out of that warning process. The device detects environmental hazards, then vibrates directly against your skin.

Different vibration patterns tell you which hazard the patch detected. Meanwhile, a related version gives robots their own form of chemical awareness.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

SELF-DRESSING CLOTHES COULD HELP OLDER ADULTS

The square patch is slightly smaller than a driver's license. That makes it compact enough to attach to clothing or place directly against the skin. Inside, a microcontroller acts as the patch's brain. A small battery powers the system. Six sensors monitor the surrounding environment for potential hazards.

The researchers designed the sensors to detect threats in the air and contaminants in water. Examples include dangerous gases and heavy metals. Once the patch detects a hazard, a tiny actuator creates a vibration against your skin. That physical alert could be harder to overlook than another phone notification.

"If you're coming into contact with a hazardous substance, you need to know as quickly as possible," said Erim Uzunoğlu, the paper's first author and a Ph.D. student at NC State. The research appears in the scientific journal Device.

Environmental sensors already exist. Many can send a warning to your smartphone. However, that approach depends on you noticing the alert. Your phone could be in a pocket, buried in a bag or silenced during work.

A physical vibration removes that extra step. The warning reaches your body as soon as the sensor detects a potential threat. Still, the researchers found that adding a small vibrating motor was not enough. The sensation had to feel strong and distinct without becoming uncomfortable.

To solve that problem, they created tiny textured surfaces between the motor and the skin. These surfaces resemble miniature patterns of raised bumps. By changing the size and spacing of the bumps, the team adjusted how each vibration felt. As a result, the alert became easier to notice. The design could prove helpful in loud environments where an audible alarm might disappear into the background.

The patch does not use the same buzzing sensation for every warning. Instead, it produces a separate haptic sequence for each hazard. One pattern might signal a dangerous gas. Another could warn about a contaminant in water.

This creates a small tactile language between the patch and the person wearing it. Therefore, you may understand the type of threat without checking a display. In proof-of-concept testing, the patch successfully detected the targeted substances. It also triggered the appropriate vibration immediately.

However, people would need time to learn what each pattern means. Clear training would become especially important in workplaces where several hazards may be present.

A wearable safety device offers little protection when its battery dies halfway through the day. To reduce that risk, the researchers placed thin-film photovoltaic cells on the patch's exterior. These cells collect solar energy while someone wears the device.

The solar cells work alongside the internal battery. At the same time, the sensors use relatively little power. During testing, that combination kept the device operating for around 24 hours. That running time could cover a full work shift. However, real-world performance would depend on sunlight, sensor activity and how someone wears the patch.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

As the team developed the wearable patch, the researchers began considering another question. Could a robot use the same tactile warning system? That idea led to an electronic skin, also called e-skin.

The robotic version places the sensor patch over a piezoelectric layer. When the patch vibrates, that movement creates an electrical signal. The robot can read the signal and identify the vibration pattern. It can then respond to the detected hazard without waiting for a wireless message.

During testing, researchers placed the e-skin on quadrupedal robots. When the robots detected chemical hazards, they changed direction and followed a safer route. This system could help robots explore locations that may be unsafe for people. It could also let a machine respond when wireless connections become unreliable.

Most robots rely heavily on cameras and digital instructions to understand their surroundings. Yet a camera cannot always identify a dangerous gas or invisible contaminant. The e-skin gives a robot another way to sense risk. More importantly, it turns the chemical warning into a physical signal within the robot's body.

That direct connection could support faster decisions. The robot would not need to transmit sensor data to a remote computer before responding. For example, a robot could inspect an industrial site while watching for leaks. It could then stop or change direction when it encounters a dangerous substance.

However, this work remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Researchers will need to test the system across harsher conditions before it can support high-risk missions.

Many experimental wearables rely on highly specialized components. Those custom parts can increase costs and slow production. In contrast, the researchers built most of this patch and e-skin with components that are already available. Only a few elements required custom engineering. That could make the technology easier to scale.

The sensor array is also modular. Developers could remove sensors that are unnecessary for a certain environment. They could then add sensors for hazards tied to a specific job or location. A water-quality worker would need a different setup than someone inspecting an area for chemical leaks.

You cannot buy this wearable hazard detection patch yet. Still, the research shows how safety alerts could move beyond screens and speakers. A vibration against your skin may reach you faster than a notification on your phone. That could become especially valuable when every second affects your exposure.

The technology may eventually help people who work near chemicals or inspect questionable water supplies. It could also support emergency teams entering places where the air may be unsafe. However, several questions remain. Researchers must determine how the patch performs after repeated wear and exposure to harsh conditions. They will also need to reduce false alarms and make each vibration easy to recognize. Comfort will play a role too. A safety patch only works when people are willing to wear it throughout the day.

NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL

A warning can only protect you when it reaches you in time. This wearable patch brings the alert directly to your skin instead of relying on a phone that you may never check. The separate vibration patterns are especially clever. They could tell you which danger is nearby before you even look at a screen. Meanwhile, the robot e-skin gives machines a physical way to recognize chemical threats and move away from them. That could eventually keep people farther from hazardous areas. The next challenge will be turning a successful laboratory prototype into something durable, comfortable and dependable enough for daily use.

"John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to 'leave town' until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER, where Republicans can then quickly pass everything they ever dreamed of, including a full and deep throated SAVE AMERICA ACT, the Budget, and the ever looming Debt Ceiling disaster, 1929! The three-fifths threshold required for cloture to end a filibuster means that Senate Republicans, even with their 53-seat majority, cannot get to 60 votes without Democrats — the procedural hurdle prevents advancing most legislation with a simple majority.

item.description: Samantha Busch shared emotional Instagram posts revealing the unbearable loneliness she faces each night, two months after Kyle Busch died from sepsis.
item.content:encoded:
It's been more than two months since Kyle Busch's sudden death, and understandably, it is not getting any easier for his widow.

In a series of Instagram Stories, Samantha Busch said some nights without her late husband are "almost unbearable."

"You’re still the last thing I see when I close my eyes and the first thing when I wake up," Busch posted on Sunday along with photos of the couple by her bedside.

"In the evenings when the kids go to bed the silence and loneliness is almost unbearable. I sleep tucked on my side of the bed with a body pillow and his shirt pretending he’s still next to me. I hate it so much that his shirt doesn’t smell like him anymore."

Busch died on May 21 after severe pneumonia turned into sepsis, sandwiched between the Coca-Cola 600 and his final victory.

The two-time NASCAR champion collapsed during a simulator session ahead of the Coca-Cola 600 and was rushed to the hospital. He died the next day.

Busch was a two-time Cup champion and undoubtedly a future Hall of Famer. He had been in the Cup Series since 2004, making 762 career starts with 63 wins.

KYLE BUSCH'S SON SUFFERS HEARTBREAK IN EMOTIONAL RETURN TO RACING AFTER FATHER'S STUNNING DEATH

The 41-year-old won the championship in 2015 and 2019, and had 234 victories across all three NASCAR national series.

Busch is the all-time record-holder for wins in both the NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts Series (102) and the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series (69).

Busch's 234th and final NASCAR win came at Dover one week before his death, when he led 147 laps in a dominating Truck Series victory.

"You never know when the last one is," Busch said after the win.

Busch's last Cup Series win came in June 2023. While he struggled for much of this season, he did start on the pole in February's Daytona 500 and was coming off a season-best finish of eighth four weeks ago at Watkins Glen.

item.title: GOP senator unveils BOASBERG Act to stop 'rogue' judges from handpicking Trump cases
item.description: Sen. Eric Schmitt's BOASBERG Act would require random assignment of federal cases and bar chief judges from influencing who hears high-profile disputes.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican is planning to curb so-called "rogue" judges, and he is using one of President Donald Trump’s greatest foils in the judicial branch as the launching point.

Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., is planning to introduce the Blocking Overt Attempts at Shopping By Enforcing Randomization Guidelines Act in an attempt to curb judge shopping in federal cases. The bill, shortened to the BOASBERG Act, is named after U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, one of Trump’s main antagonists on the bench.

Schmitt’s legislation, first obtained by Fox News Digital, would broadly require that federal cases be randomly assigned in a bid to limit the ability of judges and litigants to influence who gets to hear and oversee a case.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

"Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system," Schmitt said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts."

Schmitt’s legislation adds several guardrails to the selection process for federal cases and gives courts 120 days after enactment to implement them.

It would require the random assignment of federal civil cases, prohibit chief judges from influencing case assignments, require courts to publicly disclose their case assignment practices, create penalties for meddling with or manipulating the assignment process, and require the random reassignment of a case if the Supreme Court intervenes in a ruling.

DC APPEALS COURT ORDERS JUDGE BOASBERG TO HALT TRUMP CONTEMPT PROBE OVER DEPORTATION FLIGHTS

Boasberg, who was first appointed to the federal bench by former President Barack Obama in 2010, has become a flashpoint for Republicans and the White House for his role in several high-profile cases against Trump and his administration during his two non-consecutive stints at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.

It’s caused Trump to call for his impeachment and the Justice Department to file a misconduct claim against him.

Boasberg most recently blocked the State Department from restricting visas for foreign officials and other foreign nationals that the administration has accused of suppressing or helping suppress American free speech.

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

That latest move is just the tip of the iceberg in a long-running set of clashes between Boasberg and Trump.

Boasberg has been a key player in the administration’s attempt to deport Venezuelan migrants. He tried to temporarily block the administration’s fast-paced deportation of Venezuelan migrants that the White House alleged were Tren de Aragua gang members.

He later ordered the administration that the men had to be returned to the U.S. for violating due process in their removal.

Boasberg also landed the case surrounding "Signalgate," where top members of Trump’s Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance, War Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and then-National Security Advisor Michael Waltz, among others, accidentally included a journalist in their encrypted group message discussing strikes in Yemen.

He ordered the administration to preserve any of the messages related to the group chat, but stopped short of requiring that the administration salvage any that may have been deleted.

Schmitt hopes that his legislation will create a new operating standard moving forward.

"The BOASBERG Act prevents judges from forcing their way onto cases and is an important piece of court transparency legislation that will help restore the American people's confidence in our judiciary," Schmitt said.

item.content:encoded:
Ex-White House chief of staff to former President Barack Obama, Rahm Emanuel, said Monday that the agenda put forth by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) does not appeal to anyone outside Manhattan ahead of November's midterm elections.

Emanuel's comments followed his Wall Street Journal opinion column last week warning that "Bernie bros" and democratic socialist candidates could threaten the Democratic Party's chances in statewide and nationwide elections with unpopular policies.

He doubled down on CNN with his concerns, claiming that any election not focused on President Donald Trump would be a "dollar wasted" for Democrats.

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS NEW GENERATION OF DEM SOCIALISTS DON'T LIKE AMERICA

"This election is set up to be a referendum on Donald Trump’s corruption and his inability to manage the economy to make people‘s lives better," Emanuel said. "Anything that distracts from that means you‘re helping Donald Trump. The DSA, and that agenda it's laid out, does not play anywhere except for maybe on the upper west side of Manhattan. And any time a Democrat anywhere in a red to blue district has to either distinguish themselves rather than prosecute that the Republican would be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump is a dollar wasted."

He specifically called out DSA-backed candidates for focusing on replacing Democratic candidates in safe districts rather than putting forth effort to win races in red or purple states like North Carolina, Georgia, Arizona and Nevada.

"Do you think anybody in those states wants a member of the DSA to come campaign or any of the Progressive Caucus? And second, since 2018, the progressive caucus hasn‘t flipped a single red to blue district. And to me, this is a consequential election where we could put a checkmate on Donald Trump, and we cannot risk it with diversions from the Democratic Socialists of America, who are giving them nothing but talking points," Emanuel said.

Then you have a progressive movement, which, by the way, what is getting these guys nervous is we are winning all over this country. It’s not only Mamdani in New York City, it is in New Jersey, it’s in Ohio. It’s in Colorado. People are sick and tired of the ‘Rahm Emanuel’s’ and the Democratic establishment and the Republican establishment," Sanders said on "Face the Nation" Sunday.

Emanuel agreed with Sanders that "the system is rigged" against the middle class but emphasized that it was more important to take action rather than "talk about it."

"As I always say, the first eight letters of progressive spell 'progress,' not perfection. A lot of hot air out of Washington, not a lot of action out of it," Emanuel said.

"It was socialists who led the charge to defund the police, open the borders, abolish prisons, release violent criminals onto the streets and degrade the flag," Emanuel said.

Emanuel has a history of calling out the far-left on cultural issues that he thinks don’t play with the country at large. "We lost the plot," he said in a snippet shown on social media from the "Fifth Column" podcast in April. "We as Democrats nationally, from ‘Latinx,’ to defunding the police, to ‘Police organizations are all racist,’ to bringing a set of cultural wars to our schools. We are on the losing side of those cultural wars. Full stop."

In July, he sparred with a New Yorker interviewer over Democrats focusing on bathroom laws: "When people's backs are against the wall, they're holding on to that windowsill, and they can't make a college payment, they can't make a home mortgage payment, their healthcare is now being denied to them. They expect us Democrats to show up," he warned.

"He [Kirk] says, 'You're gonna move to Florida. It's gonna be the best thing ever. God has actually told me that this is gonna happen... you need a condo in Sarasota. Go stay there, and you can stay there for as long as you want. You never have to pay me anything. I'm never gonna ask you to leave. You just stay there and you're going to find a home here and you gonna like save your family.'"

Aside from the late Turning Point USA founder's legacy, Johnson's wide-ranging interview with Hannity also touched on family, fatherhood, America's future and more.

item.title: The welfare state broke Black families. Work can help restore the dream
item.description: Fatherlessness and dependency grew by design as welfare punished families for keeping fathers in the home, breaking the Black family for generations.
item.content:encoded:
Recently, I heard Christian Maxwell, the Republican nominee for Illinois’ 1st Congressional District, say something that I’ve been thinking about ever since. She argued that the minute Black women start seeing themselves as Americans, as fully part of the American story, the entire progressive coalition built on grievances will begin to fall apart.

Her point was that Black women have been trained, indoctrinated and propagandized to see themselves as victims of America, and that’s why progress has been stifled. They’ve been rallying around sinister influences, especially false narratives about what a Black woman is, and that’s kept them locked in a culture of poverty and resentment instead of possibility and opportunity. She’s right. And I’ve spent the past 20 years on the South Side of Chicago watching how this has happened.

In plain words, what has happened has been nothing less than a divorce. I’m not talking about marriage, but the divorce between the Black woman and the American Dream.

I say Black woman here, not to single her out, but because it is a fact. Black women have been targeted by the United States government and nonprofits over the last 60 years in ways that no other race has been.

BOB WOODSON TAUGHT ME AMERICA’S WOUNDS HEAL ONLY THROUGH TRUTH AND COURAGE

All of this happened slowly and by design. The War on Poverty promised that we would be helped, and that government programs would lift us up. But, as Shelby Steele said in "What Killed Michael Brown?" the government that had oppressed us only yesterday would now become the agent of our own uplift. There was something sinister in what he said, and he was right. Why would we expect our former oppressor to lead us to the Promised Land? Isn’t it the oppressor’s main goal to alleviate his own guilt, and would we be used in that regard?

One of the bad ideas to come out of that war was the set of rules that punished a mother for keeping a man in the house and rewarded her financially for having more children without one. We called this assistance while fatherlessness shot through the roof. What it really was was an incentive to break up the family. And it worked, as generation after generation was born into this life of dependency. It wasn’t because these families were weak, but because the system promoted dependency as the safest and most responsible choice a mother could make.

Seeing the repercussions of these policies and the continual breakdown of families saddens me. I have never met a stronger woman than a single mother raising four kids on the South Side. These women didn’t choose this system. They were born into it, and my anger has never been at them. My anger is at a bureaucracy that asked them to trust it more than they trusted themselves.

MY WALK ACROSS AMERICA IS OVER, BUT MY MISSION FOR SOUTH SIDE KIDS IS NOT

That's the work of Project H.O.O.D. We're not in the business of judgment. We're in what I call the leap business. We help mothers move from a government check that keeps them small and dependent to a paycheck that makes them whole and independent. And let me tell you, that gap is real, and I believe the government creates it on purpose to keep people trapped. Sometimes this gap is $20,000 — money that a mother has to make on her own before independence pays better than dependency. That's not only a leap of faith, but a leap toward earning more and making capitalism work for you.

I've watched a mother of four sit through electrician training and come out with a job at an electrical contracting company. Others are planning to open their own businesses. I've watched a mother of two fail the police exam twice before she passed. She now wears the badge and has become one of the best officers on her beat. I didn't do that. They did that. All we did was stand at the bottom of the gap, provide the services and resources, and then say, "We believe you can make it across."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And when they do, when that faith shows them what they are capable of and how much God has blessed them, I’m telling you, there is no look on a human face like it. Does anyone celebrate when they get a welfare check? No, but they sure celebrate when they get that paycheck, when they get an apartment of their own choosing and when they go out to a restaurant and treat themselves to a good meal. That's an American story.

That's why I believe in the trades. That's why I believe in reconnecting the Black woman and the Black family to the American Dream. That isn't charity. It's the restoration of what was already ours before the government decided it knew better.

Christian Maxwell said it plainly: The moment Black women fall in love with this country, this nation unifies like never before. I believe that too. They are the force. May God make them the force for a new day in America.
